items.title: What Is IQ? Intelligence, Cognitive Tests and Scores
items.excerpt: Understand cognitive abilities, raw scores, age norms, standard scores, percentiles and measurement uncertainty through a worked fictional example. Learn how to compare tools and choose formal assessment.

items.title: Reading EQ-60 Results: Scores, Percentiles and References
items.excerpt: Understand the numbers that appear in an EQ-60 report, follow a complete worked example, and separate scale transformations from population claims and response-quality guidance.

items.title: Emotional Intelligence: Models, Measures and Test Choices
items.excerpt: Ability tasks, emotional self-perceptions and broader emotional-social frameworks measure different things. Learn how theory, test format, scoring and version affect the choice.

items.title: Emotional Awareness and Communication: Three Practice Scenes
items.excerpt: Work through criticism, an extra request and a misunderstanding with complete conversations, observable actions and adjustments when an approach fails.

items.title: Repeated Behavior Is Not Proof of a Fixed Personality
items.excerpt: After work, you leave your running shoes by the door, yet the next day you still do not go out. On weekday mornings, though, you reliably organize your materials before a meeting. It is easy to combine those observations into a harsh judgment: “I just lack self-discipline.”
items.cover_image_alt: Repeated Behavior Is Not Proof of a Fixed Personality

items.title: The Big Five Describes Traits; RIASEC Organizes Career Interests
items.excerpt: The Big Five and RIASEC are not the same measure. The Big Five uses continuous dimensions to describe relatively stable tendencies in thinking, feeling, and behavior; RIASEC organizes the activities and work environments you would prefer to explore into six vocational-interest categories. They may be associated in group research, but are not interchangeable and cannot establish that a particular person is suited to, should pursue, or will succeed in an occupation.
items.cover_image_alt: The Big Five Describes Traits; RIASEC Organizes Career Interests

items.title: How to Read Big Five Results: Turn Descriptions into Hypotheses, Not Labels
items.excerpt: Check the scale, direction, and definitions. Turn a description into observations in two contexts, record counterexamples, and avoid fixed identity labels.
items.cover_image_alt: How to Read Big Five Results: Turn Descriptions into Hypotheses, Not Labels

items.title: Big Five Traits and Enneagram Motivation Stories Address Different Questions
items.excerpt: Big Five traits and Enneagram motivation stories address different questions. Similar terms do not establish equivalent constructs or a type conversion. Keep their sources separate when using them for reflection.
items.cover_image_alt: Big Five Traits and Enneagram Motivation Stories Address Different Questions

items.title: How Teams Can Use Big Five Language Safely: Discuss Collaboration, Not Fit Scores
items.excerpt: Use Big Five language to discuss specific teamwork needs and working agreements through voluntary conversations. Editorial examples and templates do not validate fit scores, hiring or task-allocation decisions.
items.cover_image_alt: How Teams Can Use Big Five Language Safely: Discuss Collaboration, Not Fit Scores

items.title: Examine the Sample, Measurement, Design, Uncertainty, and Causality in Big Five Research
items.excerpt: You read an article saying that “a Big Five trait is associated with a particular kind of work performance,” then encounter a louder retelling: “this personality produces that outcome.” Between those two sentences, many unspoken steps involving samples, questionnaires, time, statistical error, and causal design may already have been crossed. The most useful response when reading research is not to rush to decide whether it is true or false, but to ask: what limited inference does it actually permit me to make?
items.cover_image_alt: Illustration of a reader examining a paper beneath five magnifying glasses showing a group, questionnaires, a path, a distribution, and branching lines.

items.title: Use Big Five Results as Goal Hypotheses, Not Trait Destiny
items.excerpt: Fictional goal cards, meetings, and projects illustrate a voluntary goal, a planned condition, and observations. Everyday trials do not validate causation, individual predictions, or trait change; timing and success signals are editorial examples.
items.cover_image_alt: Use Big Five Results as Goal Hypotheses, Not Trait Destiny

items.title: Why Big Five Personality Feedback Is a “Hypothesis,” Not a “Diagnosis”
items.excerpt: Big Five feedback can offer tentative behavioral clues, not a diagnosis. Distinguish raw scores, standard scores, and percentiles, and examine descriptions against specific everyday records; personal observation is not scale or product validation.
items.cover_image_alt: An illustrative trait distribution and sliders lead to everyday observations and an editable personality hypothesis.

items.title: Observe the Sequence of a Conflict Before Discussing Personality: Do Not Reduce the Cause to Traits
items.excerpt: A fictional family-care scenario illustrates recording triggers, responses, effects, and repair attempts. Keep motives and causes uncertain; the table and script are voluntary reflection prompts, not validated interventions.
items.cover_image_alt: Two people examine four cards illustrating a trigger, opposing responses, a pause and a repair attempt.

items.title: Turn Big Five Language into Specific Communication Requests, Not Explanations of Others
items.excerpt: Fictional everyday examples illustrate asking for consent, describing one event, and making a negotiable request. The steps and tables are editorial prompts, not evidence of communication effects or relationship prediction.
items.cover_image_alt: Two people discuss colored shapes beside cards showing a clock, a chair and a listening face.

items.title: What Are the 30 Big Five Facets? Hierarchical Differences and Equivalence Traps Across NEO-PI-R, BFI-2, and BFAS
items.excerpt: The 30 facets come from the NEO-PI-R's 240 items and 6×5 structure. BFI-2 uses 15 facets, while BFAS measures 10 aspects. Identically named facets across instruments cannot be assumed equivalent. This article lists all 30 facet names and descriptive glosses across 5 domains and offers a three-step framework for comparing identically named indicators in two reports.
items.cover_image_alt: A paper tree with five colored branches stands beside diagrams showing different ways of grouping and connecting traits.

items.title: Run a Two-Week Planning-System Experiment with Observable Behavior
items.excerpt: Choose one reversible planning rule and record benefits, maintenance costs, and exceptions for two weeks. The teaching card and tables do not establish causation or match tools to Big Five scores.
items.cover_image_alt: A woman adjusting cards on a two-row planning board beside a notebook and a circular review arrow.

items.title: A 30-Day Observation and Review Plan for Big Five Results
items.excerpt: Use an editorial 30-day calendar, fictional examples, and a note card to record situations, behavior, and counterexamples. Review supports cautious reflection, not personality scoring or proof of exercise effects.
items.cover_image_alt: A person adds colored markers to a calendar-like board beneath five symbols, with an arrow showing a cycle of observation and review.

items.title: Turn Group Evidence into Reversible Experiments, Not Promises
items.excerpt: Use personality research to raise questions without overclaiming. Check group-to-person inference and use fictional examples to plan low-consequence observations, without treating associations or short-term experiences as guarantees.
items.cover_image_alt: Group research evidence linked to a cycle of individual observation, action, journaling and reflection.

items.title: Big Five Traits Are Continuums, Not Personality Boxes
items.excerpt: Big Five labels do not define fixed types. Read dimensions alongside context, observations, and counterexamples. The examples are not diagnosis or product validation.
items.cover_image_alt: A person viewing five colored continuous bands with markers, beside empty transparent boxes.

items.title: What High, Middle, and Low Big Five Ranges Mean: Start with Continuous Dimensions and the Limits of Norms
items.excerpt: What might high, middle, and low Big Five ranges mean?
items.cover_image_alt: Five colored bell-shaped curves with markers at different positions, illustrating continuous ranges rather than personality categories.

items.title: Retest Differences May Reflect Measurement, Context, and Possible Change
items.excerpt: In this fictional example, six months ago, Xiaolin completed a Big Five personality assessment. This week she took it again, and the descriptions of conscientiousness and extraversion differed. She immediately asked, “Have I changed?”
items.cover_image_alt: Two profile silhouettes on transparent panels, with colored streams representing different sources of variation.

items.title: Accommodate Different Ways of Participating in Meetings without Assigning Personality Roles
items.excerpt: Review participation with preparation, independent writing, parallel input, and decision records. The five steps and 35-minute card do not assign personality roles or guarantee outcomes.
items.cover_image_alt: Five people around a meeting table, with one speaking and others listening or taking notes.

items.title: Personality Traits Cannot Override Consent or Personal Boundaries
items.excerpt: Fictional photo-sharing and assessment-privacy scenarios show why trait labels do not grant permission. Three situations and a checklist are editorial guidance, not safety interventions or risk assessments; data-processing law has a separate scope.
items.cover_image_alt: Illustration of two women facing one another, one holding up a hand within a translucent circular boundary.

items.title: Openness and Creativity Are Related Concepts, but Not the Same Construct
items.excerpt: Openness is a broad personality trait, not by itself a score for the quality of a particular work. A fictional observation card separates trait descriptions, creative processes, and feedback while keeping task conditions and evidence limits visible.
items.cover_image_alt: Illustration of two overlapping translucent circles above an art desk, with a landscape, floating objects, and a sculptural paper form.

items.title: What Are the Five OCEAN Dimensions? Meanings, Scope, and Limits of Interpretation
items.excerpt: OCEAN offers broad coordinates for organizing recurring self-descriptions. It is not a personality ranking, fixed type, certificate of ability, or prediction of the future.
items.cover_image_alt: Illustration of people in different situations across five colored panels, representing broad personality dimensions.

items.title: How the Big Five Personality Model Took Shape: From Descriptive Words to Trait Research
items.excerpt: Understanding how the Big Five took shape requires distinguishing descriptive words, factor structure, and inventory design. Together they form a research history, not a fixed identity, causal explanation, or product validation.
items.cover_image_alt: Illustration combining archive cards, clustered dots, questionnaires, and a reader examining a form to show a path from descriptive words to measurement.

items.title: How to Read Your Full MBTI Report: From 16 Personality Results to Career, Relationships, and Communication
items.excerpt: Learn how to read a full MBTI-style report beyond the four-letter label, with career, relationship, communication, teamwork, and self-growth examples.
items.cover_image_alt: A full MBTI report reading path from 16 personality results to career, relationships, communication, and action steps

items.title: I Don’t Know What Career Is Right for Me: A Practical Career Exploration Map
items.excerpt: Not sure what career is right for you? Learn how to use RIASEC, MBTI, Big Five, and real-world validation to build a practical career exploration map.
items.cover_image_alt: 职业探索地图展示从职业兴趣、性格偏好、大五人格到现实任务验证的四步路径

items.title: Career Interest Test vs Personality Test: Which Should You Take First?
items.excerpt: Confused between career interest and personality tests? Learn how Holland Code, MBTI, and Big Five answer different career exploration questions.
items.cover_image_alt: Career exploration notes with a RIASEC structure and decision path diagram

items.title: How to Read MBTI Results: Verify the Four Preference Pairs in Real Situations
items.excerpt: Break MBTI-style results into four preference pairs, using real situations, counterexamples, and contextual changes to form tentative hypotheses rather than a fixed identity.
items.cover_image_alt: A woman compares communication, solitude, planning, and creative situations to understand MBTI preferences.

items.title: How Can MBTI Support Personal Growth? From Preferences to Four-Week Behavioral Experiments
items.excerpt: Growth isn't about becoming the opposite type, but rather practicing alternative strategies in real-world scenarios to expand the range of available behaviors.
items.cover_image_alt: A woman plans personality growth through a repeating path of observation, adjustment, and real-world practice.

items.title: What Is MBTI? What 16 Personality Types Can—and Cannot—Tell You
items.excerpt: The MBTI personality test can help you observe preferences related to energy, information gathering, decision-making, and daily organization. It cannot assess ability, diagnose a psychological condition, or determine career suitability.

items.title: Can You Study Computer Science or AI If Math Is Not Your Strength? A Course, Work-Activity, and RIASEC Checklist
items.excerpt: Can someone who struggles with math still apply to computer science or AI? Start by identifying the specific math gaps, reviewing course requirements and real work activities, and using RIASEC interests to sort majors into three working lists: keep, verify, or set aside.

items.title: FermatMind IQ Test Guide: What It Measures, How to Read Results, and Its Limits
items.excerpt: How to use FermatMind's original 30-question visual reasoning practice, read accuracy, distinguish simulated Beta from population scores, and understand limits.
items.cover_image_alt: A learner examines where IQ reasoning tools are useful across different real-life contexts.

items.title: Are Online IQ Tests Accurate? Understanding Intelligence Scores, Question Types, and Formal Assessments
items.excerpt: Understand online IQ scores, reasoning tasks, and how they differ from formal intelligence assessments. Use results for reflection, not diagnosis.

items.title: How to Interpret Online Reasoning Test Results: Scores, Question Types, Strategy, and Test Conditions
items.excerpt: Use four layers and a fictional 18/30 comparison to separate report fields, personal observations, and hypotheses, then choose a reviewable next step.
items.cover_image_alt: A young adult combines reasoning tasks, cognitive processes, and situational clues to interpret an IQ-test portrait.

items.title: IQ Test Practice and Review: A Four-Week Schedule
items.excerpt: Use an original rule example, counterexamples, error logs, and an adjustable four-week schedule to review strategies in new materials and learning tasks.
items.cover_image_alt: A learner reviews reasoning exercises, observes patterns, and plans the next stage of growth in a bright study space.

items.title: After Gaokao Scores Are Released, How Should You Shortlist Majors? A RIASEC Checklist
items.excerpt: After Gaokao rankings are released, do not jump straight to "Which major suits me?" First rule out options that fail eligibility requirements, conflict with your willingness to study the core curriculum, or rest only on popularity. Then combine RIASEC results with course fit to create three working lists: keep, verify, and set aside.

items.title: What If Parents and Students Disagree About a Major? Turn Gaokao Choice Conflicts into Three Lists
items.excerpt: When parents disagree about a major during Gaokao applications, start with shared constraints rather than arguing over who is right. Use rank, subject requirements, and enrollment plans to rule out unavailable options, then compare the remaining choices through RIASEC interests, course lists, and informational interviews.

items.title: Should You Accept Major Reassignment in Gaokao Applications? Start with the Unacceptable Majors in Each Program Group
items.excerpt: Before selecting “accept major reassignment” for a university program group, sort every major in that group into three categories: unacceptable, pending verification, or acceptable. Then use coursework, eligibility rules, and family cost constraints to decide whether the reassignment risk is one you can accept.

items.title: Is an EQ Test Accurate? EQ-60 Self-Report and Evidence
items.excerpt: EQ-60 organizes 60 self-descriptions across four dimensions. Learn what its preliminary evidence supports, how scores work and how to check an interpretation.

items.title: What Is the Enneagram? 9 Types, Core Motivations, and Reading Results
items.excerpt: The Enneagram uses nine types as a language for observing core motivations, attention habits, and stress responses. When reading results, examine your main type, nearby types, and real situations rather than asking only “which type am I?” Research offers mixed evidence for reliability and validity, so this page does not treat it as a diagnostic, hiring-screening, or career and relationship prediction tool. For tests, free-test information, questions, and access, see the dedicated test page.

items.title: Choosing a College Major After the Gaokao: How to Use RIASEC, MBTI, and Career Interest Tests
items.excerpt: Before submitting Gaokao applications, use RIASEC, MBTI, and real-world exploration as inputs—not verdicts—when comparing majors. This guide explains what these tools can and cannot tell you.

items.title: Big Five Personality Test Guide: How to Use Results and Respect Their Limits
items.excerpt: First verify the tools, scores, and comparison criteria, then use low-risk observation to gather both confirmatory evidence and counterexamples; do not let a single personality test determine ability, identity, or future.

items.title: How Should You Read a Big Five Personality Profile? Turning OCEAN Scores into a Personal Narrative
items.excerpt: Put each OCEAN dimension back into context. Map possible behaviors, costs, counterexamples, and questions to test, creating a profile you can review rather than a fixed label.

items.title: How Can Big Five Personality Results Support Growth? A Five-Dimensional Behavioral Experiment and Review Guide
items.excerpt: Do not chase ideal personality scores; instead, set a realistic goal and turn trait assumptions into observable, actionable, and reviewable behavioral experiments.

items.title: How Do You Choose a Major Track After Broad-Category Admission? Build a Pre-Enrollment Checklist with Course Directions, Holland Interests, and Major-Change Windows
items.excerpt: Before enrollment through broad-category admission, check the major list, allocation rules, core courses, and windows for changing majors. Then use Holland interests to align course tasks with future work activities.
items.cover_image_alt: 学生和家长在入学前对照大类招生分流规则、课程方向和霍兰德兴趣清单做专业方向选择

items.title: Low Conscientiousness in the Big Five: Procrastination Triggers, Task Splitting, and Execution Checklists
items.excerpt: Use a low Big Five conscientiousness result to map procrastination triggers, 15-minute task starts, feedback loops, and weekly review habits.
items.cover_image_alt: 大五人格尽责性低时，把拖延触发、任务拆分和执行复盘转成自我观察清单的桌面决策图

items.title: Low Emotional Stability in the Big Five: Stress Triggers, Recovery Habits, and Communication Boundaries
items.excerpt: Use low Emotional Stability as a stress-sensitivity signal, not a diagnosis. Map triggers, recovery habits, communication boundaries, and support signals.
items.cover_image_alt: 一位用户在压力后对照 OCEAN 结果、触发卡片和恢复清单进行自我观察的编辑插画

items.title: Disappointed With Your Admitted Major: Retake or Enroll? A Checklist of Course Costs, Transfer Windows, and Holland Interests
items.excerpt: If your admitted major disappoints you, check course boundaries, transfer windows, family costs, and aversion first. Compare enrollment, transfers, minors, postgraduate redirection, and retaking.
items.cover_image_alt: 录取专业不理想后，学生和家庭对比课程、转专业、复读成本和霍兰德兴趣的决策场景

items.title: How to Find a Job When Your Major Does Not Match: A Checklist for JD Analysis, Skill Evidence, and Internship Validation
items.excerpt: When seeking work outside your major, do not rush to close off your options. Use JD verbs, course projects, skill evidence, internship validation, and Holland interests to build a job-search path outside your major.
items.cover_image_alt: 大学生把专业课程、岗位JD、技能证据和霍兰德兴趣整理成跨专业求职路线图

items.title: Assigned to a Major You Dislike? A Course, Transfer, and Holland Recovery Checklist
items.excerpt: Do not rush to retake the entrance exam after admission to a major you dislike. Use courses, transfer policies, Holland interests, and skills bridges to judge whether it is acceptable, needs testing, or requires an alternative route.
items.cover_image_alt: 学生核对被调剂专业的课程、转专业规则、职业活动和霍兰德兴趣补救清单

items.title: Enneagram Workplace Friction: 9 Core Motivations and a Communication Conflict Toolkit
items.excerpt: Reject fixed personality labels. Examine real Enneagram stress responses to feedback, meetings, and deadlines through organizational psychology, with a 7-day ethical behavior observation checklist to clarify workplace boundaries.
items.cover_image_alt: 职场会议场景中用九型人格观察核心动机、反馈冲突、边界和压力反应的编辑风格封面图

items.title: Does a Popular Major Suit Me? A University Major Checklist Using Courses, Work Activities, and Holland Interests
items.excerpt: Look beyond popularity. Use difficult courses, real work activities, and Holland/RIASEC interests to categorize majors as retain, needs testing, or provisionally lower priority.

items.title: MBTI Personality Test: Scientific Tool or Cyber Fortune-Telling?
items.excerpt: MBTI is useful as a language for preferences, but dangerous when treated as a destiny label.
items.cover_image_alt: A glowing green node network inside a transparent cube, representing the tension between MBTI type labels and continuous personality traits.

items.title: What Is RIASEC? Understanding Holland Code Career Interests
items.excerpt: RIASEC is a career-interest model that organizes work preferences into six areas. It can help you explore career environments, but it is not a career verdict.
items.cover_image_alt: Abstract career-interest map with six work activity icons around a compass.

items.title: Why Your MBTI Type and Holland Code Results May Not Match
items.excerpt: Your MBTI and Holland Code may point in different directions because they answer different questions. Learn how to compare them safely.
items.cover_image_alt: Abstract career-interest map with six work activity icons around a compass.

items.title: How Should You Understand Different MBTI and Holland Results?
items.excerpt: Different MBTI and Holland results do not necessarily mean a test was wrong. Understanding the questions each test answers helps you use them more safely for career exploration.
items.cover_image_alt: Abstract career-interest map with six work activity icons around a compass.

items.title: Big Five Personality Test: Is It More Scientific Than MBTI—and What Can It Really Tell You?
items.excerpt: The Big Five is not a personality label. It is a five-trait map for understanding work style, stress patterns, and behavior.
items.cover_image_alt: Diagram contrasting Big Five continuous traits with MBTI type labels.

items.title: What Can a Holland Career Interest Test Tell You—and What It Cannot?
items.excerpt: A Holland test helps you understand your career-interest pattern, but it should guide exploration—not decide your future.
items.cover_image_alt: Abstract career compass with six connected directional nodes representing the RIASEC interest model and career exploration paths.

items.title: A Lower-Friction Valentine’s Day: Designing Dates with Personality and Relationship Science
items.excerpt: A good date is not necessarily expensive, crowded, or cinematic. It fits the relationship goal, stimulation threshold, and safety boundaries of the two people involved.
items.cover_image_alt: A couple plans a lower-friction date around energy, setting, and shared interests.

items.title: Why Are INFJ Men Often Considered Rare? Data Sources, Gender Norms, and Type Misinterpretation
items.excerpt: Published proportions of INFJ men depend on specific samples and instruments; gender norms may affect expression and visibility, but cannot prove that large numbers of INFJs are hidden.
items.cover_image_alt: A man observes different social roles and expression settings while reflecting on sensitivity and self-silencing.

items.title: Which Relationship Script Fits You Best? Seven Types of Love, Explained
items.excerpt: Many people think they are looking for the right person. Often, they first need to clarify what kind of relationship structure they are trying to build.
items.cover_image_alt: A couple explores different love scripts through the three paths of intimacy, passion, and commitment.

items.title: How Personality Shapes Your Attitude Toward AI: Curiosity, Anxiety, and Algorithmic Trust
items.excerpt: Your stance toward AI is not simply supportive or cautious. Personality shapes whether you treat it as a tool, a mirror, a decision aid, or a risk signal.
items.cover_image_alt: A woman weighs trust, anxiety, control, and verification skills when deciding how to use AI.

items.title: How the 16 Personality Types Talk to an AI Coach
items.excerpt: An AI coach is most useful when it helps you ask better questions, organize your thoughts, and notice blind spots. The risk is that it may agree too smoothly when you need friction.
items.cover_image_alt: A user talks with an AI coach while keeping personal judgment across different response styles.

items.title: Why Your Childhood Dream Job Still Shapes Your Career Decisions
items.excerpt: A childhood dream job does not predict your future, but it often reveals early preferences about work structure, role identity, and the life you want work to support.
items.cover_image_alt: A young adult traces career clues from childhood interests in exploring, building, and caring.

discoverability_items.title: What Is IQ? Intelligence, Cognitive Tests and Scores
discoverability_items.summary: Understand cognitive abilities, raw scores, age norms, standard scores, percentiles and measurement uncertainty through a worked fictional example. Learn how to compare tools and choose formal assessment.

discoverability_items.title: Reading EQ-60 Results: Scores, Percentiles and References
discoverability_items.summary: Understand the numbers that appear in an EQ-60 report, follow a complete worked example, and separate scale transformations from population claims and response-quality guidance.

discoverability_items.title: Emotional Intelligence: Models, Measures and Test Choices
discoverability_items.summary: Ability tasks, emotional self-perceptions and broader emotional-social frameworks measure different things. Learn how theory, test format, scoring and version affect the choice.

discoverability_items.title: Emotional Awareness and Communication: Three Practice Scenes
discoverability_items.summary: Work through criticism, an extra request and a misunderstanding with complete conversations, observable actions and adjustments when an approach fails.

discoverability_items.title: Repeated Behavior Is Not Proof of a Fixed Personality
discoverability_items.summary: After work, you leave your running shoes by the door, yet the next day you still do not go out. On weekday mornings, though, you reliably organize your materials before a meeting. It is easy to combine those observations into a harsh judgment: “I just lack self-discipline.”

discoverability_items.title: The Big Five Describes Traits; RIASEC Organizes Career Interests
discoverability_items.summary: The Big Five and RIASEC are not the same measure. The Big Five uses continuous dimensions to describe relatively stable tendencies in thinking, feeling, and behavior; RIASEC organizes the activities and work environments you would prefer to explore into six vocational-interest categories. They may be associated in group research, but are not interchangeable and cannot establish that a particular person is suited to, should pursue, or will succeed in an occupation.

items.title: IQ是什么：智力、认知测验与分数的区别
items.excerpt: 理解一般智力、不同认知任务、原始分、年龄参照常模、标准分、百分位与测量误差。通过可重算的虚构案例，判断不同工具能否比较及何时需要正式评估。

items.title: 如何练习情绪觉察、调节与沟通：三个完整场景

items.title: 情商是什么：能力型、特质型与广义模型怎样测量
items.excerpt: 同样叫情商，任务表现、自我知觉与广义情绪社会功能回答的并不是同一个问题。比较模型、工具版本和计分依据，再按目的选择测量方法。

items.title: EQ-60分数怎么看：标准分、百分位与阶段性参照

items.title: 高考志愿要不要服从调剂？先看院校专业组里的“不能接受专业”
items.excerpt: 是否服从调剂，不能脱离本省当年投档规则、目标高校招生章程和具体院校专业组回答。先列出组内全部专业，再核对选科、体检、单科、外语等硬条件，把其余专业分成“不能接受、待验证、可接受”。只有你能承担组内最坏结果时，才继续讨论是否服从调剂。本文提供决策清单，不预测录取，也不替代官方填报规则。

items.excerpt: 看到一篇“最新研究改写大五人格”的新闻，最容易发生的两种反应是立刻相信，或立刻否定。两者都太快。研究发表得新，只说明它进入了可讨论的记录，并不说明它已经替代了较早的证据；一篇论文也可能认真、重要，却只回答一个窄问题。更稳妥的做法是把它放回背景： 它具体问了什么，采用什么工具、样本与设计，估计有多大且有多少不确定性，独立

items.title: 检查大五研究的样本、测量、设计、不确定性与因果

items.title: 信度与效度是证据问题，不是质量徽章
items.excerpt: 当人格测试页面写着“可靠”“有效”时，读者很容易把它理解成一句总评：这份测试已经准确地说明了我是谁。这个理解太快了。 信度 关心的是：在明确的测量条件下，分数是否具有某种一致性； 效度 关心的是：已有证据是否支持把这些分数解释为某件事，并用于某个明确用途。两者都是需要说明对象、证据和边界的测量术语，不是贴在任何人格产品

page.title: About FermatMind
page.summary: Who we are, what we build, and the standards behind our assessment product.
page.content_md:
## Our mission

FermatMind builds practical assessment tools for personality insight, growth planning, and role-fit reflection.

We focus on clear interpretation language that can be applied in real decisions, not abstract labels.

## Assessment approach

- Structured questionnaires with transparent scoring logic

- Readable reports focused on behavior and decision implications

- Iterative quality review across item wording and flow completion

## Privacy and safety boundary

FermatMind reports are designed for education and self-reflection. They are not medical diagnosis and do not replace professional care.

We avoid absolute claims and continuously align product practice with applicable privacy principles.

page.title: Our Team
page.summary: A cross-functional team covering psychometrics, product, engineering, and content quality.
page.content_md:
## Core functions

- Psychometrics and content: framework design, item quality, interpretation tone

- Product and UX: completion flow, clarity, and usability validation

- Engineering and data: reliability, privacy controls, and secure delivery

- Support and operations: policy handling, issue triage, and response workflow

## How we work

We ship in small, testable iterations and prioritize measurable clarity improvements.

When user risk is involved, we choose conservative language and explicit boundaries.

page.title: 关于 FermatMind
page.summary: 我们是谁、做什么，以及测评产品背后的方法边界。
page.content_md:
## 我们的目标

FermatMind 聚焦人格洞察、成长规划与角色匹配，提供可执行的测评工具。

我们强调可读、可用、可落地的解释语言，而不仅是标签化结论。

## 测评方法

- 结构化问卷与透明评分逻辑

- 结果解释聚焦行为表现与决策影响

- 持续优化题项表达与流程完成率

## 隐私与安全边界

FermatMind 报告用于教育和自我认知，不是医疗诊断，也不替代专业治疗建议。

我们避免绝对化承诺，并按适用情形持续对齐隐私保护原则。

page.summary: 由心理测量、产品、工程与内容质量共同协作的跨职能团队。

## 核心分工

- 心理测量与内容：框架设计、题项质量、解释口径

- 产品与体验：流程设计、可理解性与可用性验证

- 工程与数据：稳定性、隐私控制与安全交付

- 支持与运营：政策处理、问题分级与反馈闭环

## 协作方式

我们以小步可验证方式持续迭代，优先解决影响用户决策质量的问题。

涉及风险的场景采用更保守表达与更明确的使用边界。
